summary: A 1979 paper describing a datagram-based query and response service for host names and addresses, provided by the ARPANET Network Information Center. It was a new way to distribute and update host name and address information.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of everyone keeping a name list, you ask a helper computer, and it tells you the address.

questions: how did early networks look up host addresses
subtitle: A datagram-based service for looking up host addresses on demand.

tldr.problem: Networks needed a way to keep host addresses current as the network grew, without distributing enormous address lists to every machine.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC Name Server accepts simple datagram queries asking for a host's address and responds with the address directly, using only a lightweight transaction-based protocol.
tldr.outcome: The service showed that dynamic query-and-response was practical for address distribution and opened the door to future directory services on the Internet.

today: RFC 756 is an historic specification describing an experimental service that ran in 1979. The approach of dynamic query-and-response for addressing information was superseded by the Domain Name System (DNS), which became the standard for Internet host name resolution.

sections.title: The Problem with Centralized Host Tables
sections.content:
In the early ARPANET, every host kept a complete list of all other hosts on the network and their addresses. As the network grew, maintaining and distributing this list became a burden. Hosts with limited memory could not keep an up-to-date copy, and refreshing the list on thousands of machines took time and resources.

The NIC Name Server (RFC 756) proposed a new approach: instead of pushing a huge table to every host, let each host query a central service when it needs to know a host's address.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if everyone in a city had to keep a printed phone book. When it changes, printing and mailing new books to everyone is expensive. Instead, ask an operator who can look it up for you.

sections.title: How the Service Works
sections.content:
A host needing to reach another host sends a short datagram (a single independent packet) to the Name Server with the name of the target host. The Name Server looks up the address in its database—maintained by the ARPANET's Network Information Center at SRI International—and sends back the address in a datagram response.

The protocol is simple: the query contains a network name and a host name (for example, !ARPANET!FOO-TENEX), and the response contains the target address as four numeric octets. When no exact match is found, the server can return a list of similar names to help the user correct a typo.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a postcard asking 'where is Alice?' and the post office mails you back her address.

sections.title: Practical Uses and Limitations
sections.content:
By 1979, the Name Server was running on an ARPANET host and serving a provisional service. Mobile packet radio terminals used it to bootstrap their operation: at startup, they held only the address of a few name servers, queried for the addresses they needed, and then opened connections. TENEX hosts used an interactive interface to demonstrate the concept.

The RFC discusses extensions that were considered: queries for services rather than just hosts, options to return data in different formats, and ways to handle replies too large for a single datagram. These ideas anticipated many features of modern directory services.
sections.plainLanguage: A lonely computer in the field only needed to remember a few phone numbers, could call and ask for others, and never had to carry the whole phone book.
